title: Brief madness
hook: anger is a brief madness, Seneca begins his book on it (On Anger 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Canus at the board, counting the pieces as the centurion waited. Your line was finish the game. Did you finish one thing before reacting? Day five hundred three.
screen: `CANUS AT THE BOARD — FINISH THE GAME.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time you were truly angry. Not annoyed. Angry. Now try to remember your face. You probably can't, because you weren't looking at it. Everyone else was. Seneca's older brother Novatus once asked him to write about how anger might be calmed. Seneca answered with three whole books, and he starts the first one not with a definition but with a mirror. Of all the passions, he says, anger is the ugliest and the wildest. And then he borrows a phrase from older philosophers that has stuck for two thousand years. Today: brief madness.
screen: `TRY TO REMEMBER YOUR ANGRY FACE.` → `A BROTHER ASKS FOR HELP.` → `THREE BOOKS, STARTING WITH A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: First, the phrase. Some wise men, Seneca writes, have called anger a brief madness. In Latin, brevis insania. Like madness, it forgets decency, ignores friendship, won't listen to reason, and charges at what it wants even when the charge will hurt itself. The only difference is that it passes. Usually. Second, the mirror. Seneca describes the angry face in close-up, and it's not flattering: eyes blazing, face flushing as the blood rushes up, lips trembling, teeth clenched, breath hissing, hands clapping together, feet stamping. You can't tell, he says, whether this vice is more hateful or more ugly. He wants Novatus to see what everyone else sees. Third, the body knows first. Notice that Seneca's list is all body. Long before we decide we're angry, the jaw has tightened, the heat has risen, the voice has gotten louder. Those are the first signs, and they're the useful ones, because they show up while there's still a gap before the words come out. Fourth, why this matters now. Seneca will spend three books on what to do about anger. But the start is simply recognizing it. You can't step out of a madness you don't notice you're in. A short madness is still a madness: a texted reply, a slammed door, a sentence you can't take back, all inside ninety seconds. Naming it as madness, while it's happening, is the first crack of light.
screen: `SOME WISE MEN: A BRIEF MADNESS.` · `THE ANGRY FACE, IN CLOSE-UP.` · `THE BODY KNOWS FIRST.` · `NAME IT WHILE IT'S HAPPENING.` · then, large: `BRIEF MADNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring back a recent moment of anger, a small one. Replay it slowly, but don't follow the story. Follow your body. Where did it start? A hot face, a tight jaw, a quick breath, fists, a jump in your voice? Find your first sign: the one that shows up before anything else. Now breathe out slowly and let that part of your body soften. Remember where it is. That's your early-warning bell. The bell holds the time.
Brief madness. Seneca's opening to On Anger: some wise men called anger a brief madness, deaf to reason, ugly in the face. Today's word.
Your line: brief madness. Today, the first time you feel your early-warning sign, name it quietly: brief madness. That's all. Just the name. Day five hundred three.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca's On Anger often learn their own first bodily signs of anger and name them as they happen, to catch anger before it speaks.

original.note: Latin, 'a brief madness': the old phrase for anger that Seneca opens his book with.

trapdoor: what you thought: anger is just a strong feeling.
what it means: Seneca calls it a brief madness, deaf to reason, and starts with how it looks in the body.
what a scholar hears: Novatus was later adopted and took the name Gallio, the same Gallio who in Acts 18 refuses to hear a case against Paul in Corinth.

notes: On Anger 1.1 paraphrased: written for Novatus; anger the most hideous and frenzied passion; 'quidam itaque e sapientibus viris iram dixerunt brevem insaniam'; the description of the angry face and body. Confirm; the Latin is given in the nominative form 'brevis insania' for the games.
Novatus = Lucius Junius Gallio Annaeanus, proconsul of Achaia in Acts 18. Confirm; also used on day 509 for On the Happy Life.
The 'ninety seconds' figure is illustrative, not a scientific claim.
